prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and timely problem: standard NLI benchmarks such as SNLI and MultiNLI are known to contain annotation artifacts and shallow cues that inflate measured performance, yet constructing better evaluation sets usually requires manual or adversarial data collection. The paper proposes an automated alternative: characterize existing examples into difficulty strata using training-dynamics features collected from models trained on the evaluation split itself, including both premise+hypothesis and hypothesis-only settings, then use clustering to isolate a “hard” subset that is intended to be less artifact-driven and more realistic. The paper also applies the same machinery to training-set filtering and reports that reduced subsets can match or exceed full-data performance on the Naik et al. stress tests.

Overall, I found the paper interesting and potentially useful. The central idea—using training dynamics plus hypothesis-only behavior to identify likely shortcut-heavy versus genuinely difficult examples—is intuitive and reasonably novel in the NLI evaluation context. The empirical patterns are also compelling at a high level: the hard subsets are much smaller, substantially lower-performing for strong encoders, and much closer to chance for hypothesis-only models. The paper is clearly motivated, and the attempt to avoid manually constructed artificial stress tests is valuable.

That said, I also have substantial concerns about methodology, framing, and the strength of the claims. My main reservation is that the proposed “test set characterization” relies on training directly on the test set to obtain training dynamics. Although the authors state that this is only for characterization and not for classifier evaluation, this still makes the resulting benchmark definition model-dependent and split-dependent in a way that is unusual for evaluation methodology. In effect, the benchmark is being defined using supervised access to the labels of the evaluation set and optimization on those same examples. This does not invalidate the descriptive analysis, but it weakens the claim that the method provides a generally better test set for model evaluation. At minimum, the paper should discuss much more explicitly what evaluation protocol is envisioned in practice. If every new benchmark requires training on the test labels to define itself, then the method is better understood as a post hoc diagnostic tool for existing datasets than as a deployable benchmark-construction pipeline.

Relatedly, the claim of model-agnosticism is overstated. The paper shows some transfer between RoBERTa- and DeBERTa-derived splits, which is useful, but the splits are still induced from specific trained models and their calibration/training dynamics. The cross-model results in Table 4 do suggest some consistency, yet they also show fairly large differences, especially for ambiguous and hard subsets in MultiNLI. This is evidence of partial robustness, not full model independence. I would encourage the authors to soften the language and characterize the method as relatively stable across similar encoder families rather than model-agnostic.

A second major concern is whether the hard split truly corresponds to “fewer spurious correlations” rather than simply “examples that are harder for the chosen models.” The paper uses a small set of heuristics—word overlap, antonyms, length mismatch, misspellings, negation—to support the claim that spurious correlations are reduced. This is directionally reasonable, but these heuristics capture only a narrow slice of known NLI artifacts. In particular, hypothesis-only artifacts are often lexical, stylistic, and label-conditional in ways not reducible to these five measures. The fact that hypothesis-only accuracy drops on the hard split is stronger evidence than the heuristic analysis, but even that does not fully distinguish between “artifact-free” and “distributionally unusual or annotation-noisy.” The manual examples are suggestive, yet anecdotal. I would have liked to see stronger validation, for example: comparison against known artifact annotations if available; human judgments of naturalness and correctness across splits; or analysis of whether the hard split is enriched for annotation disagreement or mislabeled examples. The limitations section explicitly says the method is unsuitable for identifying mislabeled examples, but in practice hard-to-learn examples often include label noise, and the paper does not convincingly disentangle this from genuine reasoning difficulty.

There are also some technical and statistical issues that need clarification. The variability formula in Equation (2) appears incorrect as written: it seems to omit the square in the variance term. If this is only a typesetting mistake, it should be fixed. More broadly, the paper does not provide enough detail on the GMM setup: covariance type, initialization, number of random restarts, sensitivity to random seed, and whether three clusters were fixed a priori or validated empirically. Since the cluster sizes are highly imbalanced and central to the conclusions, robustness analyses are important. It would also help to compare against simpler alternatives: for example, clustering using only P+H dynamics, only H dynamics, only Data Maps features, or even thresholding hypothesis-only confidence. Without such ablations, it is hard to know how much of the gain comes from the full 8-feature design versus the obvious signal that hypothesis-only learnable examples are artifact-prone.

The statistical testing section is also not fully convincing. The paper mentions Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction, but the reporting is vague. It is unclear exactly which pairwise comparisons are being tested, how many tests are performed, and where the corrected p-values are reported. The statement “we found evidence for the presence of moderate spurious correlations (p=0.04) in the hard split between the three classes” is difficult to interpret, since Mann-Whitney is a two-sample test and “between the three classes” suggests multiple comparisons. The paper would benefit from a more precise statistical analysis and clearer reporting of effect sizes, not just significance.

The training-set characterization results are promising but also somewhat hard to interpret. The paper evaluates filtered training subsets on the Naik et al. stress tests and reports that some subsets outperform full-data training. This is interesting, but the connection between the proposed test-set characterization objective and the training-set filtering objective is not fully developed. Why should the same clustering notion of easy/ambiguous/hard be optimal for training selection? Also, the comparisons to Data Maps and AUM may not be entirely fair because the baselines are instantiated with somewhat ad hoc thresholds, while the proposed method uses a learned clustering and multiple subset combinations. A stronger baseline section would include more careful tuning of baseline subset sizes and perhaps random subsets matched for size. As written, the claim of “surpassing other dataset characterization techniques” feels stronger than the evidence supports.

I also have concerns about the FEVER experiments. FEVER is not a standard sentence-pair NLI dataset in the same sense as SNLI/MultiNLI, and the paper itself notes that the premise/hypothesis structure is atypical. The hypothesis-only baseline on FEVER is near chance when trained conventionally, but much higher when trained on the dev set itself, which suggests the dynamics there may reflect memorization or dataset-specific peculiarities rather than the same artifact phenomenon studied in SNLI/MultiNLI. The FEVER results are interesting as an exploratory extension, but they do not strongly support the main claims and may distract from the cleaner NLI story.

On the positive side, I think the paper’s empirical observations are meaningful. The monotonic degradation from easy to ambiguous to hard is consistent across datasets and models. The hard subsets are indeed challenging for strong encoders while remaining composed of naturally occurring examples rather than synthetic perturbations. This is a useful contribution even if one interprets the method primarily as a diagnostic lens over existing benchmarks rather than a turnkey benchmark-construction method. I also appreciate that the authors compare P+H and H-only dynamics and that they attempt cross-model validation.

For improvement, I would strongly recommend the following. First, reframe the contribution more conservatively as post hoc benchmark diagnosis and subset extraction, unless the authors can articulate a practical protocol for constructing evaluation sets without problematic use of test labels. Second, add ablations showing the contribution of each feature group and of the GMM itself. Third, provide robustness analyses over seeds and clustering hyperparameters. Fourth, strengthen validation that the hard split is not merely noisy: manual annotation of a sample for label correctness and naturalness would go a long way. Fifth, improve the baseline comparisons for training-set filtering, including random subsets and better-tuned Data Maps/AUM baselines. Sixth, clarify the statistical testing and fix the apparent formula issue.

In terms of writing, the paper is generally readable, but there are several places where the claims are too broad relative to the evidence. Phrases like “more accurate measure of model performance in the real world,” “model-independent,” and “minimizes spurious correlations” should be toned down. The method likely reduces some detectable artifacts and yields harder subsets; that is already a worthwhile result. There are also a few grammatical issues and minor inconsistencies that should be cleaned up in revision.

My overall assessment is that this is a promising paper with an interesting idea and useful empirical findings, but the current version overclaims and leaves important methodological questions unresolved. If accepted, it should be on the basis of its value as a diagnostic and data-characterization study rather than as a definitive solution for constructing unbiased NLI test sets. If rejected, I would still encourage the authors to continue this line of work, because with stronger validation and clearer framing it could become a solid contribution.

I lean borderline positive on novelty and empirical interest, but borderline negative on methodological rigor and claim support.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes an automated method to characterize NLI datasets into easy/ambiguous/hard subsets using training-dynamics features. For each test example, the authors train models directly on the test split in two settings—premise+hypothesis and hypothesis-only—and extract 8 features (confidence, variability, correctness, AUM in both settings). A Gaussian Mixture Model clusters examples into three difficulty levels, which are then interpreted as a harder stress-test-like benchmark. Experiments on SNLI, MultiNLI, and FEVER show that the hard subsets yield much lower accuracy and lower hypothesis-only performance, which the authors interpret as reduced spurious correlations. The same characterization idea is also applied to training data, where selected subsets reportedly match or exceed full-data performance on Naik et al.'s stress tests while using less data.
strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: standard NLI benchmarks contain annotation artifacts and shortcut correlations that inflate performance.
The core idea of using training dynamics plus hypothesis-only behavior to characterize examples is intuitive and potentially useful for identifying shortcut-heavy instances.
The method is relatively simple to implement and does not require manual construction of adversarial examples.
The paper evaluates on multiple datasets (SNLI, MultiNLI, FEVER) and includes some cross-model comparison with RoBERTa and DeBERTa.
The training-set filtering experiments are potentially interesting, suggesting that training-dynamics-based subset selection may improve data efficiency.
The paper attempts to connect difficulty splits with heuristic artifact measures and reports statistical testing.
weaknesses: The central methodology for test-set characterization is scientifically problematic because it trains directly on the test set to derive features, which compromises the notion of a clean evaluation benchmark and makes the resulting hardness definition partly circular.

The claimed reduction of spurious correlations is not rigorously established; lower model accuracy or lower hypothesis-only accuracy does not by itself prove fewer artifacts, only greater difficulty for the chosen models.

The method is not convincingly model-agnostic: the characterization depends on model outputs, calibration, optimization dynamics, and architecture, and the cross-model evidence is limited and somewhat inconsistent.

The clustering design appears under-justified: the number of clusters is fixed to three, cluster ranking is based only on average confidence, and there is little ablation on feature choices, covariance structure, initialization sensitivity, or alternative clustering methods.
The paper conflates several notions—difficulty, ambiguity, artifact prevalence, and realism—without clearly distinguishing them or validating them against human judgments.
Empirical comparisons to prior methods are limited and not fully fair; for example, Data Maps and AUM baselines are reduced to ad hoc thresholding choices without strong tuning or broader baselines.
The hard subsets are heavily label-skewed toward neutral, so reduced performance may partly reflect label-distribution shift rather than cleaner evaluation.
The FEVER setup is not fully convincing as an NLI benchmark, and the premise/hypothesis role description appears confusing or reversed in places.
methodological_flaws: Equation (2) for variability appears mathematically incorrect: the variance term is written without squaring the deviation, i.e., sqrt(sum(p-mean)/E) instead of sqrt(sum((p-mean)^2)/E) or an unbiased variant. If this is not a typographical error and was implemented as written, the feature is invalid; if it is only a typo, it still raises concerns about mathematical care.

The method trains models on the test set to compute training dynamics for that same test set. This creates a form of target leakage/circularity: examples are deemed easy or hard based on how easily the model can fit them when directly optimized on them. Such a procedure does not characterize benchmark difficulty independently of memorization dynamics and undermines claims about constructing a principled evaluation set.

The main claim that the hard split has fewer spurious correlations is insufficiently supported. The evidence relies largely on lower hypothesis-only accuracy and a few shallow heuristics (word overlap, antonyms, negation, misspellings, length mismatch). These heuristics are incomplete proxies and do not establish causal reduction of artifacts.

The statistical analysis is weakly specified. The paper mentions Mann-Whitney-U tests across classes/difficulty levels, but it is unclear exactly which pairwise comparisons are performed, what effect sizes are, and whether independence assumptions hold under multiple correlated heuristic measures. Reporting only p-values such as p=0.04 as evidence of 'moderate spurious correlations' is not rigorous.

The interpretation of clusters as easy/ambiguous/hard based solely on intra-cluster average confidence from the P+H model is ad hoc. No validation is provided that GMM components correspond to semantically meaningful difficulty strata rather than artifacts of feature scaling or class imbalance.

The claim of model independence is overstated. Training dynamics are known to depend on architecture, optimization, calibration, and random seed. The paper provides only limited cross-model transfer and no seed variance analysis. Table 4 also shows substantial discrepancies across source characterizations, especially for ambiguous/hard splits.

The training-set filtering evaluation uses Naik et al.'s stress tests as the main downstream metric, but these stress tests are themselves acknowledged by the authors to amplify artifacts unrealistically. This weakens the logic of claiming improved real-world data quality from better performance on those tests.

Potential confounding from label imbalance is not adequately controlled. The hard split contains many more neutral examples; thus lower accuracy and lower heuristic prevalence may partly arise from changed class composition rather than true artifact removal. Per-class balanced evaluations or matched-control analyses are missing.

There is no convincing demonstration that the proposed hard subsets are more 'realistic and diverse linguistic phenomena' beyond anecdotal manual inspection. No human evaluation, phenomenon annotation, or external benchmark correlation is provided.

Baseline selection for Data Maps and AUM appears somewhat arbitrary (e.g., percentile choices for 'ambiguous' subsets), which may bias comparisons in favor of the proposed method. Stronger baselines such as confidence-based filtering, influence-based methods, or artifact classifiers are absent.
